## 1. Radiation basics and units
### Ionising vs non-ionising
- **Ionising**: X-rays (radiographs, fluoroscopy, CT, DEXA) and gamma rays (nuclear medicine).
- **Non-ionising**: **MRI** (radiofrequency energy in a magnetic field) and **ultrasound** (sound waves).

### Units
| Quantity | Unit | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Absorbed dose** | **Gray (Gy)** = 1 joule per kg (old unit rad; 1 Gy = 100 rad) | Energy deposited in tissue |
| **Equivalent dose** | **Sievert (Sv)** (old unit rem; 1 Sv = 100 rem) | Absorbed dose x radiation weighting factor (1 for X-rays and gamma rays, 20 for alpha particles) |
| **Effective dose** | **Sievert (Sv)**, usually mSv | Equivalent dose x **tissue weighting factors**, summed; estimates whole-body stochastic risk |
| **Activity** | **Becquerel (Bq)** (old unit curie) | One radioactive disintegration per second |

### Biological effects
| Effect | Threshold | Severity | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Deterministic (tissue reactions)** | **Has a threshold**; severity rises with dose | Dose-dependent | Skin erythema (about 2 Gy), epilation (about 3 Gy), desquamation, **cataract** (ICRP threshold lowered to **0.5 Gy** in 2011), sterility |
| **Stochastic** | **No threshold** (linear no-threshold model); **probability** rises with dose | All-or-none | **Cancer** (leukaemia, thyroid, breast), heritable effects |

- Most radiosensitive tissues: **bone marrow, gonads, lens, thyroid, breast**; children are more sensitive than adults (longer life expectancy, dividing cells).

### Typical effective doses (approximate)
| Examination | Effective dose | Equivalent in background radiation |
|---|---|---|
| **Extremity radiograph** (hand, foot, knee) | Under 0.01 mSv | Under 1.5 days |
| **Chest radiograph (PA)** | About 0.02 mSv | About 3 days |
| **Pelvis / hip radiograph** | About 0.5-0.7 mSv | About 3 months |
| **Lumbar spine radiographs** | About 1-1.5 mSv | About 6 months |
| **DEXA** | About 0.001-0.01 mSv | Less than a day |
| **CT head** | About 2 mSv | About 8 months |
| **CT chest / CT lumbar spine** | About 6-7 mSv | About 2-3 years |
| **CT abdomen and pelvis** | About 8-10 mSv | About 3-4 years |
| **Tc-99m bone scan** | About 4-6 mSv | About 2 years |
| **FDG PET-CT** | About 10-25 mSv | Several years |

- **Natural background** radiation averages about **2.4 mSv per year** worldwide (about 3 mSv in the USA, mainly radon).
- **CT gives far higher doses than radiographs**: one CT abdomen is equivalent to several hundred chest radiographs.

## 2. Production of X-rays and the radiograph
### The X-ray tube
- **Cathode** (heated tungsten filament) releases electrons by **thermionic emission**; electrons are accelerated across a high voltage to the **anode** (tungsten target, rotating to spread heat).
- About **99% of the energy becomes heat**, only about 1% X-rays.
- X-rays are produced by:
  - **Bremsstrahlung ("braking") radiation**: electrons decelerated by the nuclei of target atoms; produces a continuous spectrum; **the main source**.
  - **Characteristic radiation**: incident electron ejects an inner-shell electron; an outer electron drops in and emits a photon of fixed energy.
- **Filtration** (aluminium) removes low-energy photons that would only add skin dose.

### Exposure factors
| Factor | Controls | Effect of increasing it |
|---|---|---|
| **kVp (peak kilovoltage)** | **Energy (quality, penetration)** of the beam | More penetration, **less contrast** (more grey), more scatter |
| **mA x time (mAs)** | **Quantity** (number of photons) | Darker film, **dose rises in direct proportion** |
| **Source-to-image distance** | Intensity follows the inverse square law | Less magnification, sharper image, needs more mAs |

### Interactions with tissue
- **Photoelectric effect**: photon is completely absorbed by an inner-shell electron. Probability is roughly proportional to **Z cubed / E cubed** (atomic number cubed, energy cubed).
  - Dominant at **low energies** and in **high-atomic-number** materials (**bone - calcium, iodine and barium contrast, lead**).
  - Responsible for **image contrast** and for patient dose.
- **Compton scatter**: photon interacts with an outer-shell electron, loses part of its energy and **changes direction**.
  - Dominant at **higher energies** in soft tissue.
  - **Main source of occupational dose to staff** and of image fog; reduced by **collimation** and anti-scatter **grids**.
- **Attenuation** depends on thickness, density and atomic number: order of radiodensity on a radiograph from black to white: **air, fat, soft tissue/fluid, bone, metal**.
- **Magnification** increases with object-to-detector distance; standard calibration markers (25 mm ball) are used for arthroplasty templating (radiographs typically magnify about 15-20%).
- Digital radiography: computed radiography (photostimulable phosphor plates) and direct digital radiography (flat-panel detectors).

## 3. Fluoroscopy and radiation protection in theatre
### Image intensifier (C-arm) principles
- The **X-ray tube (source)** and the **image intensifier / flat-panel detector** sit on opposite ends of the C.
- **Scatter is greatest on the tube (entrance) side** of the patient, because most scattering occurs where the beam enters.
  - Place the **tube under the table** and the **image intensifier on top, close to the patient**.
  - For a lateral view, the surgeon should stand on the **image intensifier side**, not the tube side.
- **Patient skin dose** is highest at the beam entrance; keeping the tube far from the patient and the intensifier close to the patient reduces both patient dose and scatter.
- **Magnification (zoom) modes and inverting the C-arm** (tube on top) increase dose to patient and staff.
- **Mini C-arms** give much lower doses; useful for hand and foot surgery.

### ALARA ("as low as reasonably achievable"): time, distance, shielding
- **Time**: short screening bursts, **pulsed fluoroscopy** (low frame rate), **last-image hold**, the surgeon directing each shot.
- **Distance**: dose follows the **inverse square law** - **doubling the distance from the source reduces the dose to one-quarter**. Scatter at 1 m from the patient is about 1/1000 of the entrance dose; step back at least 1-2 m during screening.
- **Shielding**:
  - **Lead apron** of **0.25-0.5 mm lead equivalent** (0.5 mm attenuates about 95% or more of scatter); wraparound aprons for staff who turn their back.
  - **Thyroid collar** (thyroid is highly sensitive), **lead glasses** (cataract risk), mobile lead screens.
  - **Lead gloves give false security**: with the hand in the primary beam, automatic brightness control increases output and overall dose; **keep hands out of the beam**.
- **Collimation**: narrows the beam, reduces dose and scatter, sharpens the image.
- **Dosimeters** (film badge, TLD, OSL): worn under the apron at the chest/waist, with a second over the collar at neck level where available; ring dosimeters for hands.
- The **hands** of orthopaedic surgeons receive the highest dose (direct beam exposure in fluoroscopy-heavy procedures such as distal locking and percutaneous fixation).

### Dose limits (ICRP recommendations; national regulations, e.g. India's AERB, follow these closely)
| Group | Annual effective dose limit |
|---|---|
| **Occupational (radiation worker)** | **20 mSv per year averaged over 5 years**, not more than **50 mSv in any single year** |
| **Lens of the eye (occupational)** | **20 mSv per year** averaged over 5 years (reduced from 150 mSv in 2011) |
| **Skin, hands and feet (occupational)** | **500 mSv per year** |
| **General public** | **1 mSv per year** |
| **Pregnant worker (after declaring pregnancy)** | **1 mSv to the fetus** for the remainder of pregnancy |

### Pregnancy and radiation
- Fetal risk depends on **gestational age** and dose:
  - First 2 weeks: **all-or-none** effect (loss or normal development).
  - **8-15 weeks**: highest risk of CNS effects (microcephaly, intellectual disability).
- Fetal doses **below about 50 mGy (5 rad)** are not associated with an increased risk of malformations or fetal loss (ACOG; 100 mGy is often quoted as the threshold for deterministic effects); stochastic childhood cancer risk is small but not zero.
- Radiographs of the extremities, chest and cervical spine give negligible fetal dose; **necessary imaging should not be withheld**. CT abdomen-pelvis gives roughly 10-25 mGy to the fetus.
- Shield, collimate, and prefer **ultrasound or MRI without gadolinium** where suitable.

> Exam pearl: Scatter (Compton) is greatest on the X-ray tube side - keep the tube under the table, the intensifier close to the patient, and stand on the intensifier side. Doubling distance quarters the dose. Occupational limit 20 mSv/year (averaged over 5 years), lens 20 mSv, extremities 500 mSv, public 1 mSv, pregnant worker 1 mSv to the fetus.

## 4. Computed tomography (CT)
- A rotating X-ray tube and opposite detector array; attenuation data are reconstructed into cross-sectional images (filtered back-projection or iterative reconstruction).
- **Helical (spiral) multidetector CT**: continuous table movement; allows thin slices and **multiplanar (MPR) and 3D reconstructions**.
- **Pitch** = table movement per rotation / beam width: higher pitch = faster scan, lower dose, lower resolution.
- **Hounsfield units (HU)**: attenuation relative to water.

| Tissue | Approximate HU |
|---|---|
| **Air** | **-1000** |
| **Fat** | **-100 to -50** |
| **Water** | **0** (by definition) |
| **Soft tissue / muscle** | +20 to +60 |
| **Acute blood** | +50 to +80 |
| **Cancellous bone** | +300 to +700 |
| **Cortical bone** | +1000 or more |
| **Metal** | Several thousand (beyond the scale) |

- **Windowing**: **window width** (range of HU displayed - narrow for soft tissue, wide for bone) and **window level** (centre).
- Opportunistic osteoporosis screening: low HU of L1 cancellous bone (thresholds around 110-135 HU are quoted) correlates with low BMD.
- **Metal artefact** (streaks) from **beam hardening** (low-energy photons absorbed preferentially) and **photon starvation**:
  - Reduce with **higher kVp and mAs**, thinner reconstructions, **metal artefact reduction (MAR) algorithms**, **dual-energy CT** with virtual monochromatic images.
  - **Titanium causes less artefact than stainless steel or cobalt-chrome**.
- Other artefacts: partial-volume averaging, motion, ring (detector fault).
- **Orthopaedic uses**: complex articular fractures (tibial plateau, pilon, calcaneus, acetabulum), scaphoid union, spine trauma (CT is first-line in adult high-risk cervical spine injury - NICE/Canadian C-spine rule), bone tumour matrix and cortex, CT angiography, rotational profile (femoral anteversion, tibial torsion), preoperative planning and navigation.
- **CT dose index (CTDIvol)** and **dose-length product (DLP)** are the dose descriptors displayed by the scanner.
- **Iodinated contrast**: risk of contrast-induced nephropathy (hydrate; check eGFR), allergic-like reactions; **metformin** may need withholding in renal impairment.

## 5. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA)
- **Two X-ray beams of different energies** allow subtraction of soft tissue and calculation of **areal BMD (g/cm2)** - a 2D measurement, not true volumetric density.
- **Sites**: **lumbar spine (L1-L4)**, **total hip and femoral neck**; **distal one-third (33%) radius** if spine or hip cannot be measured, in **hyperparathyroidism**, or in very obese patients.
- **T-score**: number of SDs from the mean of **young healthy adults** (peak bone mass) - used for **postmenopausal women and men aged 50 or over**.
- **Z-score**: SDs from the mean of **age- and sex-matched** people - used for **premenopausal women, men under 50 and children**; **Z-score -2.0 or lower = "below the expected range for age"** (look for secondary causes).

| WHO category (T-score) | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Normal** | **-1.0 or higher** |
| **Osteopenia (low bone mass)** | **Between -1.0 and -2.5** |
| **Osteoporosis** | **-2.5 or lower** |
| **Severe (established) osteoporosis** | **-2.5 or lower plus one or more fragility fractures** |

- **Falsely high spine BMD**: **degenerative osteophytes**, facet arthritis, **aortic calcification**, vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, laminectomy defects, contrast, metal.
- Each **1 SD fall in BMD roughly doubles fracture risk** (about 1.5-3 times, site-dependent).
- Serial scans should be on the same machine; a change must exceed the **least significant change** (about 2.8 x precision error).
- **FRAX** estimates 10-year probability of hip and major osteoporotic fracture from clinical risk factors with or without femoral neck BMD. **Trabecular bone score (TBS)** adds microarchitecture information from spine DEXA.

## 6. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
### Principles
- Patient placed in a strong static magnetic field (**B0**, measured in **tesla**; clinical 1.5 T and 3 T); **hydrogen protons** align with the field and precess at the **Larmor frequency** (proportional to field strength; about 64 MHz at 1.5 T).
- A **radiofrequency (RF) pulse** tips the protons; when it stops, they relax and emit a signal detected by receiver coils. **Gradient coils** localise the signal (and cause the noise).
- **T1 (spin-lattice, longitudinal) relaxation**: recovery of longitudinal magnetisation; **fat has a short T1 (bright on T1)**.
- **T2 (spin-spin, transverse) relaxation**: decay of transverse magnetisation; **water has a long T2 (bright on T2)**.
- **TR** (repetition time) and **TE** (echo time) determine weighting.

| Sequence | TR / TE | Fat | Fluid / oedema | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **T1-weighted** | **Short TR, short TE** | **Bright** | Dark | **Anatomy, marrow replacement** (tumour, infection, fracture line), fatty atrophy, lipomas, post-gadolinium |
| **T2-weighted** | **Long TR, long TE** | Intermediate (bright on fast spin echo) | **Bright** | **Pathology**: oedema, effusion, tears, cysts |
| **Proton density (PD)** | **Long TR, short TE** | Bright | Intermediate-bright | **Menisci, articular cartilage, labrum** (high resolution) |
| **STIR** | Inversion recovery nulls fat | **Dark (suppressed)** | **Very bright** | **Marrow oedema** (occult fractures, stress reactions, osteomyelitis, bone bruise); robust near metal |
| **Fat-saturated T2 / PD** | Chemical fat suppression | Dark | Bright | Bone bruises, tendon and cartilage lesions |
| **Gradient echo (GRE / T2-star)** | No 180-degree refocusing pulse | Variable | Bright | Cartilage; **"blooming" of haemosiderin** (pigmented villonodular synovitis / TGCT) and metal; worst artefact near implants |

- **Always dark (low signal) on all sequences**: **cortical bone, tendons, ligaments, menisci/fibrocartilage, air, fibrous tissue, haemosiderin, calcification** (few mobile protons or very short T2).
- Normal adult marrow is fatty (bright T1); children have more red marrow (intermediate T1). **Marrow darker than adjacent muscle or disc on T1** suggests replacement (tumour, infection, myeloma).

### Contrast (gadolinium)
- Paramagnetic agent that **shortens T1** -> enhancing tissue becomes **bright on T1** (use with fat suppression).
- Uses: **abscess vs phlegmon** (rim enhancement), tumour viability and extent, synovitis, scar vs recurrent disc after surgery (**scar enhances; recurrent disc does not, apart from its rim**), **MR arthrography** (dilute intra-articular gadolinium for **labral tears** of hip and shoulder, and partial rotator cuff tears).
- **Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis** with older linear agents in severe renal impairment (**eGFR under 30**); macrocyclic agents are safer. Gadolinium deposits in the brain with repeated linear-agent doses. **Avoid gadolinium in pregnancy** unless essential.

### Artefacts (classic exam topic)
| Artefact | Cause | Example and fix |
|---|---|---|
| **Magic angle** | Tendons with collagen fibres oriented at **about 55 degrees to B0** show increased signal on **short-TE sequences** (T1, PD, GRE) | **Supraspinatus**, peroneal tendons at the lateral malleolus, patellar tendon: mimics tendinopathy/tear; **disappears on T2 (long TE)** |
| **Susceptibility (metal)** | Ferromagnetic or metallic implants distort the local field: signal void and bright rim, geometric distortion | **Worst with stainless steel and cobalt-chrome; least with titanium and tantalum**; worst on GRE and chemical fat saturation. Fix: **fast spin echo**, **STIR instead of fat-sat**, increase receiver bandwidth, thinner slices, lower field (1.5 T rather than 3 T), **MARS** sequences (SEMAC, MAVRIC), orient implant along B0 |
| **Chemical shift** | Fat and water protons precess at slightly different frequencies | Black or bright band at fat-water interfaces in the frequency-encoding direction (e.g. vertebral endplates) |
| **Motion / pulsation** | Patient movement, vessels, CSF | Ghosting in the phase-encoding direction |
| **Truncation (Gibbs)** | Sharp high-contrast boundaries | Line within the meniscus mimicking a tear; or within the spinal cord mimicking a syrinx |
| **Partial volume** | Thick slices averaging structures | Pseudotears; use thinner slices |

### Safety
- **Absolute contraindications** (unless labelled MR conditional): **non-MR-conditional cardiac pacemakers and defibrillators**, **ferromagnetic intracranial aneurysm clips**, **cochlear implants**, some neurostimulators, **metallic foreign body in the orbit** (screen welders/grinders with orbital radiographs).
- **Orthopaedic implants** (titanium, cobalt-chrome, stainless steel) are generally **safe at 1.5 T and 3 T** once in place, but produce artefact; **external fixators** may be ferromagnetic and can heat - check MR conditional status. Implanted spinal cord stimulators and growth rods (magnetically controlled growing rods) have specific restrictions.
- **Projectile** risk from ferromagnetic objects; **RF heating** (specific absorption rate, SAR) and burns from looped cables; acoustic noise (ear protection).
- MRI is safe in **any trimester of pregnancy** when indicated (non-contrast).

### Orthopaedic indications in brief
- **Investigation of choice** for: **occult hip fracture** (NICE: MRI if radiographs negative; CT if MRI unavailable within 24 h), **occult scaphoid fracture**, **early osteonecrosis** (most sensitive; **double-line sign** on T2), stress fractures, **early osteomyelitis and discitis**, soft-tissue and bone tumour **local staging**, spinal cord compression and cauda equina, ligament, meniscus and cartilage injury.
- **Transient osteoporosis of the hip**: diffuse marrow oedema without a subchondral line (vs AVN).

## 7. Ultrasound
- **Piezoelectric crystals** in the transducer convert electrical energy to sound and back; speed of sound in soft tissue about **1540 m/s**.
- **Frequency vs penetration**: **higher frequency = better resolution but less depth**.
  - **High-frequency linear probes (about 7-18 MHz)** for superficial musculoskeletal structures (tendons, nerves, small joints).
  - **Low-frequency curvilinear probes (2-5 MHz)** for deep structures (adult hip, obese patients).
- Echogenicity: **hyperechoic** (bright - bone cortex, calcification, fibrillar tendon), **hypoechoic**, **anechoic** (black - simple fluid).
- **Artefacts**:
  - **Anisotropy**: tendons and ligaments appear **falsely hypoechoic when the beam is not perpendicular** to the fibres - mimics tendinopathy or tear; correct by angling (heel-toe) the probe.
  - **Posterior acoustic shadowing** behind bone, calcification, gas.
  - **Posterior acoustic enhancement** behind fluid-filled cysts (ganglion, Baker cyst).
  - Reverberation (comet-tail) from metal and needles.
- **Doppler** (colour and power): hyperaemia in synovitis, infection, **neovascularity in tendinopathy**; vascular assessment.
- **Advantages**: no radiation, cheap, portable, **dynamic examination** (snapping hip, tendon subluxation, impingement), comparison with the other side, **guided injections, aspiration and biopsy**, regional anaesthetic blocks. **Operator-dependent**; cannot penetrate bone.
- Paediatric uses: **DDH (Graf method; alpha angle 60 degrees or more normal)** in infants up to about 4-6 months (before the femoral head ossific nucleus blocks the view), **hip effusion** in the irritable hip/septic arthritis, subperiosteal abscess.
- Adult uses: rotator cuff tears (accuracy similar to MRI for full-thickness tears in expert hands), Achilles and patellar tendon, Morton neuroma, soft-tissue masses (initial triage), foreign bodies (including radiolucent wood), nerve entrapment (median nerve cross-sectional area in carpal tunnel syndrome).

## 8. Nuclear medicine
### Radionuclides
| Agent | Physical half-life | Mechanism and use |
|---|---|---|
| **Technetium-99m (Tc-99m) MDP / HDP** | **6 hours**; pure **gamma emitter, 140 keV** | Diphosphonate adsorbed onto **hydroxyapatite (chemisorption)**; uptake reflects **osteoblastic activity and blood flow** |
| **Indium-111 labelled leukocytes** | About **2.8 days (67 hours)** | Autologous WBCs labelled in vitro; infection (acute, neutrophil-mediated); imaged at 24 h |
| **Tc-99m HMPAO labelled leukocytes** | 6 hours | Alternative WBC label; better image quality, lower dose |
| **Tc-99m sulfur colloid** | 6 hours | Marrow imaging; combined with labelled WBC scan |
| **Gallium-67 citrate** | About **78 hours** | Binds transferrin/lactoferrin; infection and inflammation; **spine osteomyelitis/discitis** (WBC scan is poor in the spine) |
| **F-18 FDG (PET)** | **About 110 minutes** | Glucose analogue taken up by metabolically active cells (tumour, infection, inflammation); **sarcoma staging and treatment response, spinal infection** |
| **F-18 sodium fluoride (PET)** | About 110 minutes | Bone turnover; more sensitive than MDP for metastases |

### Three-phase bone scan
| Phase | Timing | Reflects |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Flow (angiographic / dynamic)** | **Immediately**, first 1-2 minutes | Arterial perfusion |
| **2. Blood pool (soft-tissue)** | **About 5 minutes** | Capillary/extracellular blood pool (hyperaemia) |
| **3. Delayed (bone)** | **2-4 hours** | Bone turnover (osteoblastic activity) |

- **Osteomyelitis**: increased uptake in **all three phases**, focal on the delayed phase.
- **Cellulitis**: increased uptake in phases 1 and 2, diffuse and **not focal in the bony phase**.
- **Fracture**: positive within **24-72 hours** in most patients (may be delayed in the elderly); can remain positive for 1-2 years.
- **SPECT** (and SPECT-CT) improves localisation (e.g. spondylolysis, facet arthropathy, osteoid osteoma).
- **Cold (photopenic or falsely negative) lesions**: **multiple myeloma**, **Langerhans cell histiocytosis** (often), very aggressive purely lytic metastases (**renal cell and thyroid carcinoma**), early **avascular necrosis**, early osteomyelitis in neonates or infarcted bone, sites of radiotherapy.
- **Superscan**: diffuse intense skeletal uptake with **faint or absent kidneys** - diffuse osteoblastic metastases (**prostate, breast**) or metabolic bone disease (**hyperparathyroidism, renal osteodystrophy**, osteomalacia).
- Other hot patterns: **osteoid osteoma** (intense focal uptake; **double-density sign**), Paget disease (intense uptake of an expanded bone, "Mickey Mouse" vertebra), stress fractures, CRPS (periarticular uptake on delayed images), heterotopic ossification maturity (decreasing activity indicates maturity before excision).
- **Bone scan in arthroplasty**: periprosthetic uptake is **normal for about 1 year after THA and longer (1-2 years or more) after TKA**; a **normal bone scan effectively excludes loosening or infection** (high NPV), but a positive scan is non-specific.
- **Combined labelled leukocyte and sulfur colloid marrow scan** is the most accurate nuclear technique for PJI (**about 90% accuracy**): infection shows WBC uptake **without** matching marrow uptake (incongruent).
- Note: the 2018 ICM/MSIS criteria rely on serum and synovial markers, not imaging, for diagnosing PJI.

> Exam pearl: T1 = short TR/short TE, fat bright; T2 = long TR/long TE, water bright; STIR is the most sensitive for marrow oedema and works near metal. Magic angle at 55 degrees on short-TE sequences disappears on T2. Titanium gives the least artefact on CT and MRI. Tc-99m: half-life 6 h, 140 keV; cold lesions = myeloma, LCH, renal and thyroid metastases.

pharmacology and perioperative care.md:
## 1. Preoperative assessment and optimisation
### ASA physical status
| ASA | Definition | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **I** | Normal healthy patient | Fit young adult |
| **II** | Mild systemic disease | Controlled hypertension or diabetes, smoker, BMI 30-40 |
| **III** | Severe systemic disease | Poorly controlled diabetes, COPD, BMI 40 or more, dialysis |
| **IV** | Severe systemic disease that is a **constant threat to life** | Recent MI (under 3 months), severe valve disease, sepsis |
| **V** | Moribund, not expected to survive without the operation | Ruptured aortic aneurysm |
| **VI** | Brain-dead organ donor | - |

- Suffix **E** for emergency surgery. ASA III or more independently predicts complications and mortality (including after hip fracture).

### Cardiac risk
- **Revised Cardiac Risk Index (Lee)**: high-risk surgery, ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, **insulin-treated diabetes**, **creatinine over 2 mg/dL**. Each adds risk.
- **Functional capacity under 4 METs** (cannot climb two flights of stairs) = higher risk.
- **Coronary stents**: defer elective surgery at least **30 days after a bare-metal stent** and ideally **6 months (minimum) to 12 months after a drug-eluting stent**; continue aspirin perioperatively where possible; never stop dual antiplatelet therapy early without cardiology input.
- **Aortic stenosis**: risk of hypotension with neuraxial anaesthesia and bone cement implantation syndrome; echocardiography for an undiagnosed murmur before elective surgery.

### Modifiable risk factors before elective arthroplasty and fixation
| Factor | Threshold / action |
|---|---|
| **Diabetes** | HbA1c above about **7.5-8%** is associated with PJI and wound complications (ICM: no single cut-off agreed); **fructosamine above about 290 micromol/L** is a better short-term predictor; perioperative glucose **over 200 mg/dL** increases infection |
| **Malnutrition** | **Albumin under 3.5 g/dL**, **transferrin under 200 mg/dL**, **total lymphocyte count under 1500 cells/mm3** - increased wound complications and PJI; optimise before elective surgery |
| **Obesity** | **BMI 40 or more** markedly increases PJI, wound problems and revision; counsel and optimise |
| **Smoking** | Stop **at least 4 weeks** (ideally 6-8) before surgery: nicotine vasoconstriction, carbon monoxide; higher wound infection, nonunion, PJI |
| **Staphylococcus aureus carriage** | About 20-30% of people carry it nasally; screen and **decolonise: nasal mupirocin 2% twice daily for 5 days plus chlorhexidine body washes** |
| **Anaemia** | WHO definition Hb **under 13 g/dL in men, under 12 g/dL in women**; investigate and treat (oral or **IV iron**) before elective surgery |
| **Dental** | Routine antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures in patients with joint replacements is **not** generally required (AAOS/ADA); treat active dental sepsis before arthroplasty |
| **Intra-articular steroid** | Avoid within about **3 months** before arthroplasty of that joint (higher PJI) |
| **Inflammatory arthritis** | See section 7; **cervical spine flexion-extension radiographs in rheumatoid arthritis** (atlantoaxial instability) before intubation; also screen in **Down syndrome** and some skeletal dysplasias |

## 2. Antibiotics
### Mechanisms and key toxicities
| Class / drug | Mechanism | Orthopaedic points and toxicity |
|---|---|---|
| **Beta-lactams** (penicillins, **cephalosporins**, carbapenems) | Bind penicillin-binding proteins, **inhibit cell-wall synthesis** (bactericidal) | **Cefazolin** = standard prophylaxis; MRSA resistant via **PBP2a (mecA gene)** |
| **Vancomycin** (glycopeptide) | Binds D-Ala-D-Ala, blocks cell-wall synthesis | MRSA; slow infusion (over 1-2 h) to avoid **vancomycin flushing ("red man") syndrome**; nephrotoxic; heat-stable, used in cement |
| **Aminoglycosides** (gentamicin, tobramycin) | **30S** ribosome, protein synthesis | Gram-negative; **nephrotoxic and ototoxic**; heat-stable in cement |
| **Clindamycin** | **50S** ribosome | Penicillin-allergic prophylaxis; anaerobes; **C. difficile colitis** |
| **Linezolid** | 50S (blocks initiation complex) | MRSA/VRE, excellent oral bioavailability; **myelosuppression** (over 2 weeks), serotonin syndrome, neuropathy |
| **Tetracyclines** (doxycycline) | 30S | Tooth staining and bone deposition in children |
| **Fluoroquinolones** (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) | **DNA gyrase / topoisomerase IV** | Good bone penetration and oral bioavailability; **tendinopathy and Achilles rupture** (risk higher with age over 60 and corticosteroids), arthropathy in growing animals |
| **Rifampicin** | **RNA polymerase** | **Active against biofilm** (staphylococcal implant infection); **never as monotherapy** (rapid resistance); enzyme inducer (reduces warfarin, oral contraceptives); orange secretions |
| **Co-trimoxazole** | Folate synthesis | Oral step-down; hyperkalaemia, marrow suppression |
| **Daptomycin** | Cell-membrane depolarisation | MRSA; **raised CK / myopathy** |

### Surgical prophylaxis (clean orthopaedic surgery)
- **Cefazolin 2 g IV** (**3 g if 120 kg or more**), infused **within 60 minutes before incision** and **before tourniquet inflation**.
- **Vancomycin** (15 mg/kg) for MRSA carriers or high-risk settings: start **within 120 minutes** before incision; usually combined with cefazolin rather than replacing it (vancomycin is less effective against MSSA).
- **Penicillin allergy**: cefazolin can be used unless there is a history of a severe immediate (IgE-mediated) reaction (anaphylaxis); cross-reactivity is low (about 1-2%). Alternatives: clindamycin 900 mg or vancomycin.
- **Redose cefazolin every 4 hours** of surgery or after **blood loss over 1500 mL**.
- **Duration: no longer than 24 hours** after surgery (CDC 2017 recommends no additional doses after closure in clean procedures). Prolonged prophylaxis increases resistance and C. difficile without benefit.
- **Antibiotic-loaded cement**: heat-stable powders (**gentamicin, tobramycin, vancomycin**); low dose for prophylaxis (about 1 g per 40 g cement), high dose (several grams per 40 g) for spacers; liquid antibiotics weaken cement.

### Open fractures
- Give **as soon as possible - ideally within 1 hour of injury** (BOAST 4: within 1 hour; co-amoxiclav or cefuroxime, or clindamycin if penicillin allergic).
- Classic US regimen: **first-generation cephalosporin** for Gustilo I and II; **add gram-negative cover (aminoglycoside)** for type III; **add penicillin for farmyard or faecal contamination (Clostridium)**.
- Duration: **until 72 hours after injury or 24 hours after definitive wound closure, whichever is sooner** (BOAST 4).
- **Tetanus** prophylaxis according to immunisation status (toxoid, plus tetanus immunoglobulin for tetanus-prone wounds in incompletely immunised patients).

### Skin preparation and theatre
- **Hair removal by clipping, not shaving**, just before surgery (shaving causes microabrasions and higher SSI).
- **Chlorhexidine-alcohol** was superior to aqueous povidone-iodine in clean-contaminated surgery (Darouiche, NEJM 2010).
- Orthopaedic trauma (PREP-IT programme): **PREPARE (NEJM 2024)** - **iodine povacrylex in alcohol** had fewer SSIs than chlorhexidine in alcohol for **closed** fractures, with no difference for open fractures; **Aqueous-PREP** - no difference between aqueous povidone-iodine and aqueous chlorhexidine for open fractures.
- Laminar airflow, limited traffic, double gloving, normothermia, glycaemic control and avoiding unnecessary transfusion all reduce SSI.

## 3. Venous thromboembolism (VTE)
- Without prophylaxis, **venographic DVT** occurs in roughly **40-60%** after THA, TKA and hip fracture surgery; symptomatic VTE is much less common.
- **Virchow triad**: stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability.
- Highest-risk orthopaedic patients: hip fracture, arthroplasty, major trauma, pelvic fractures, spinal cord injury, previous VTE, malignancy, thrombophilia, oestrogen therapy, obesity, immobilisation.

### Anticoagulants
| Drug | Mechanism | Monitoring | Reversal | Key points |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Unfractionated heparin** | Potentiates **antithrombin** -> inhibits **thrombin (IIa) and Xa** equally | **aPTT** | **Protamine** (full) | Short half-life, safe in renal failure; higher **HIT** risk |
| **LMWH** (enoxaparin, dalteparin) | Antithrombin-mediated, **mainly anti-Xa** | **Anti-Xa** levels (rarely needed) | Protamine (**partial**, about 60%) | Renally cleared - reduce dose if CrCl under 30 mL/min |
| **Fondaparinux** | Synthetic pentasaccharide, **indirect Xa inhibitor** via antithrombin | Anti-Xa (specific) | **No specific reversal**; not reversed by protamine | **No HIT**; renally cleared; long half-life |
| **Warfarin** | Inhibits **vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1)** -> reduces factors **II, VII, IX, X** and **proteins C and S** | **INR** (target 2-3) | **Vitamin K** (slow) plus **4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate** (rapid); FFP if PCC unavailable | Early **procoagulant** state (protein C falls first) - bridge in high-risk; **warfarin skin necrosis**; many interactions (rifampicin, antibiotics) |
| **Rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban** | **Direct Xa inhibitors** | Not routinely | **Andexanet alfa**; PCC | Oral, fixed dose; rivaroxaban 10 mg once daily, apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily for arthroplasty prophylaxis |
| **Dabigatran** | **Direct thrombin (IIa) inhibitor** | Not routinely (thrombin time) | **Idarucizumab** (specific antibody); dialysable | Mainly renal excretion |
| **Aspirin** | **Irreversible COX-1 acetylation** -> less thromboxane A2 | - | Platelet transfusion | Effect lasts the platelet lifespan (**7-10 days**) |

- **Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT type II)**: immune (IgG against **heparin-platelet factor 4** complex); platelets fall over 50% at **5-10 days**; paradoxical **arterial and venous thrombosis**. Stop all heparin; give a non-heparin anticoagulant (**argatroban**, fondaparinux or a DOAC); do not give platelets or start warfarin until platelets recover.

### Guidelines for prophylaxis
- **NICE NG89 (2018, updated 2019)**:
  - **Elective hip replacement**: LMWH for 10 days followed by **aspirin for 28 days**, or LMWH for 28 days (with stockings), or **rivaroxaban**.
  - **Elective knee replacement**: **aspirin for 14 days**, or LMWH for 14 days (with stockings), or rivaroxaban.
  - **Fragility fracture of the pelvis, hip or proximal femur**: **LMWH (from 6-12 h after surgery) or fondaparinux (from 6 h after surgery) for 1 month**.
  - **Lower-limb immobilisation** (cast) and arthroscopy: consider LMWH if VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk.
- **ACCP (2012)**: for THA/TKA any of LMWH (preferred), fondaparinux, DOACs, low-dose heparin, warfarin, aspirin or intermittent pneumatic compression; **minimum 10-14 days, extended up to 35 days**.
- **AAOS (2011)**: pharmacological and/or mechanical prophylaxis; **no specific agent mandated**; **routine postoperative duplex screening not recommended**; **IVC filter** only if VTE with contraindication to anticoagulation.
- **CRISTAL (JAMA 2022)**: cluster-randomised, aspirin vs enoxaparin after THA/TKA - **aspirin had a higher rate of symptomatic VTE** (mainly below-knee DVT); no difference in PE or death. Aspirin remains an accepted option in lower-risk patients (debated).
- **Mechanical**: early mobilisation, **intermittent pneumatic compression**, foot pumps; graduated stockings (contraindicated in peripheral arterial disease).

### Anticoagulation and neuraxial anaesthesia (ASRA)
- **Prophylactic LMWH**: at least **12 hours** between last dose and spinal/epidural needle insertion or catheter removal; **therapeutic LMWH: 24 hours**.
- First postoperative prophylactic LMWH dose at least **12 hours after needle placement** and at least **4 hours after catheter removal** (ASRA 2018).
- **Clopidogrel** stopped **5-7 days**, ticagrelor 5 days, prasugrel 7 days before neuraxial block; **aspirin alone is not a contraindication**.
- **Rivaroxaban/apixaban** stopped about **72 hours** before neuraxial block (ASRA); **warfarin**: INR normal.
- Risk of **spinal epidural haematoma**: new back pain, leg weakness, numbness - urgent MRI and decompression (ideally within 8 hours).

## 4. Blood management and tranexamic acid
### Tranexamic acid (TXA)
- **Synthetic lysine analogue**; reversibly **blocks the lysine-binding sites on plasminogen**, preventing its binding to fibrin -> **antifibrinolytic**.
- **AAOS/AAHKS/ASRA/AHS clinical practice guidelines (2018) for THA and TKA**:
  - **IV, topical and oral TXA all reduce blood loss and transfusion**; no clear difference between routes.
  - Single and multiple doses are similarly effective; doses of **1 g IV or about 10-20 mg/kg** before incision are typical.
  - TXA **does not increase VTE risk** in the general arthroplasty population; evidence in very high-risk patients (recent stent, previous VTE) is limited - individual decision.
- **CRASH-2 (Lancet 2010)**: TXA in bleeding trauma patients reduced all-cause and bleeding death when given **within 3 hours** of injury (1 g over 10 min then 1 g over 8 h); **after 3 hours it increased bleeding deaths**.
- Contraindications/cautions: active arterial or venous thrombosis, hypersensitivity, history of seizures (high doses), severe renal impairment (dose adjust).

### Transfusion
- **Restrictive thresholds** are standard: **Hb 7 g/dL** generally; **8 g/dL** in patients with cardiovascular disease or symptoms.
- **FOCUS trial (NEJM 2011)**: hip fracture patients with cardiovascular disease/risk factors - **liberal (Hb under 10) vs restrictive (symptoms or Hb under 8)** transfusion: **no difference in death or ability to walk at 60 days**.
- **Patient blood management**: treat preoperative anaemia (IV iron), TXA, meticulous haemostasis, **cell salvage** (contraindicated in infection and malignancy; acceptable to many Jehovah's Witnesses in a continuous circuit), restrictive transfusion.
- Transfusion risks: **transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI)** (commonest cause of transfusion-related death in many series), **TACO** (circulatory overload), haemolytic reactions (ABO incompatibility - clerical error), infection, immunomodulation (higher SSI/PJI).

## 5. Analgesia and anaesthetic pharmacology
### Multimodal analgesia (reduces opioid use)
- **Paracetamol** (regular), **NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor** (if no contraindication), **regional blocks/local infiltration**, **single-dose dexamethasone** (reduces pain and PONV), opioids for breakthrough only.
- **Gabapentinoids**: modest benefit with sedation and respiratory depression risk; not routinely recommended in consensus guidelines (debated).
- **Regional techniques**:
  - **Adductor canal block** for TKA: **preserves quadriceps strength** compared with femoral nerve block (lower fall risk); often with **IPACK** (posterior capsule).
  - **Local infiltration analgesia (LIA)** (Kerr and Kohan) for THA/TKA.
  - **Fascia iliaca or femoral nerve block** for **hip fracture** (NICE recommends a nerve block at presentation/surgery).
  - Interscalene block for shoulder surgery: **phrenic nerve palsy almost always** (ipsilateral hemidiaphragm) - caution in respiratory disease; Horner syndrome, hoarseness.
- Concern that regional blocks or epidurals **mask compartment syndrome** (e.g. tibial fractures, forearm fractures in children): use low-concentration local anaesthetic, close monitoring, compartment pressure measurement where doubt (debated).

### NSAIDs
- Inhibit **COX-1** (constitutive: gastric mucosa, platelets, renal blood flow) and **COX-2** (inducible: inflammation; also required for normal **fracture healing** - COX-2 knockout mice show impaired healing).
- Clinical effect on fracture and spinal fusion healing is **debated**; short courses at standard doses appear safe; avoid prolonged high doses in nonunion-prone situations.
- **Heterotopic ossification prophylaxis**: **indomethacin 75 mg/day for about 6 weeks** (some use shorter courses) or **single-dose radiotherapy 7-8 Gy** within **24 hours before or 72 hours after surgery** (acetabular fracture via Kocher-Langenbeck or extended approaches; THA in high-risk patients - previous HO, ankylosing spondylitis, DISH, hypertrophic OA).
- Adverse effects: GI ulceration, renal impairment (avoid with ACE inhibitors and diuretics - "triple whammy"), asthma, platelet dysfunction (non-selective), cardiovascular events (COX-2 selective and high-dose diclofenac).

### Opioids
- **Mu-receptor agonists**: respiratory depression, sedation, constipation, nausea, urinary retention, pruritus, delirium; reverse with **naloxone**.
- **Codeine and tramadol** are activated to their active metabolites via **CYP2D6** - **ultra-rapid metabolisers** risk toxicity (codeine contraindicated in children under 12); poor metabolisers get little analgesia.
- **Tramadol**: also serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibition - **serotonin syndrome** (with SSRIs) and lowered seizure threshold.
- Prolonged opioid use before arthroplasty predicts worse outcomes and more complications; opioid-induced hyperalgesia.

### Local anaesthetics
- Block **voltage-gated sodium channels** from inside the axon; the **unionised form crosses the membrane**. In **acidic (infected) tissue** more drug is ionised -> **less effective**.
- **Amides** (two "i"s: lidocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine, prilocaine) - hepatic metabolism; **esters** (procaine, chloroprocaine, tetracaine) - plasma cholinesterase; PABA metabolite causes allergy.
- **Small fibres (pain, temperature, autonomic) are blocked before large motor fibres**.

| Drug | Commonly quoted maximum dose (plain) | With adrenaline | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Lidocaine** | **3-4.5 mg/kg** (sources vary) | **7 mg/kg** | Fast onset, intermediate duration; Bier block (0.5% plain) |
| **Bupivacaine** | **2 mg/kg** (about 150 mg) | About 2.5 mg/kg | Long acting; **most cardiotoxic**; **never for IV regional (Bier) block** |
| **Ropivacaine** | **3 mg/kg** | - | Less cardiotoxic, more motor-sparing |
| **Prilocaine** | 6 mg/kg | 8 mg/kg | Agent of choice for Bier block; **methaemoglobinaemia** |

- **Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST)**: CNS first (**perioral tingling, tinnitus, metallic taste**, agitation, **seizures**) then cardiovascular (arrhythmias, collapse); bupivacaine may cause cardiac arrest without warning.
  - Management: stop injection, call for help, airway and 100% oxygen, **benzodiazepine** for seizures, **20% lipid emulsion: 1.5 mL/kg bolus then infusion** (0.25 mL/kg/min, ASRA), reduced adrenaline doses (under 1 microgram/kg), avoid vasopressin, prolonged CPR (consider cardiopulmonary bypass).
- **Bier block (IVRA)**: double cuff; **tourniquet must stay inflated at least 20-30 minutes** after injection to avoid a toxic bolus.
- **Chondrotoxicity**: continuous intra-articular infusion (pain pumps) of **bupivacaine** linked to **glenohumeral chondrolysis**; dose- and time-dependent toxicity to chondrocytes (bupivacaine and lidocaine more than ropivacaine).
- Adrenaline in digital blocks (1:100,000-1:200,000) is safe in healthy fingers (Lalonde; WALANT); phentolamine reverses ischaemia.

### Malignant hyperthermia
- **Autosomal dominant**; mutation of **RYR1** (ryanodine receptor, sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release channel) in most; CACNA1S in a few.
- **Triggers: volatile anaesthetics and succinylcholine**.
- Signs: **earliest = unexplained rise in end-tidal CO2**, tachycardia, **masseter spasm**, generalised rigidity, hyperkalaemia, acidosis, rhabdomyolysis (myoglobinuria, raised CK); **hyperthermia is a late sign**.
- Treatment: stop triggers, hyperventilate with 100% oxygen, **dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV** (repeat to effect; blocks calcium release from RYR1), cool, treat hyperkalaemia and arrhythmias.
- Associations: **central core disease**, King-Denborough syndrome. Diagnosis: **in vitro caffeine-halothane contracture test** on muscle biopsy.
- **Duchenne and other dystrophies**: succinylcholine causes **hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest** (rhabdomyolysis); avoid succinylcholine (and volatile agents are generally avoided) - not classic MH.
- **Spina bifida and myelodysplasia**: **latex allergy** - latex-free theatre.

## 6. Bone-active drugs
| Drug | Mechanism | Key facts |
|---|---|---|
| **Bisphosphonates** (alendronate, risedronate, ibandronate, **zoledronate**) | Pyrophosphate analogues binding hydroxyapatite; **nitrogen-containing** agents inhibit **farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase** (mevalonate pathway) -> loss of GTPase prenylation -> osteoclast dysfunction and apoptosis. Non-nitrogen (etidronate, clodronate) form toxic ATP analogues | Oral: fasting, upright 30 min, poor absorption (under 1%); avoid if CrCl under 35. **HORIZON Recurrent Fracture Trial**: IV zoledronate 5 mg yearly started within 90 days after hip fracture repair reduced new clinical fractures and **all-cause mortality**. Adverse: oesophagitis, acute-phase reaction (IV), hypocalcaemia (correct vitamin D first), **osteonecrosis of the jaw** (rare, mainly high-dose oncology), **atypical femoral fractures**. **Drug holiday** considered after about 5 years oral / 3 years IV in lower-risk patients |
| **Denosumab** | **Human monoclonal antibody against RANKL** (mimics osteoprotegerin) | 60 mg SC every 6 months (**FREEDOM** trial); not renally cleared; **stopping causes rebound bone loss and multiple vertebral fractures** - follow with a bisphosphonate; hypocalcaemia. 120 mg monthly for **giant cell tumour of bone** and skeletal metastases |
| **Teriparatide** | Recombinant **PTH 1-34**; **intermittent** daily dosing is **anabolic** (continuous PTH is catabolic) | 20 micrograms SC daily, traditionally for up to 2 years (US boxed warning removed in 2020); **osteosarcoma in rats** -> avoid in **Paget disease, open physes, prior skeletal radiotherapy, unexplained raised ALP, bone malignancy, hypercalcaemia**. May aid fracture healing (off-label, debated). Follow with antiresorptive |
| **Abaloparatide** | **PTHrP analogue** | Anabolic; similar cautions |
| **Romosozumab** | **Monoclonal antibody against sclerostin** (increases Wnt signalling) | **Dual action**: increases formation, decreases resorption; monthly for 12 months; **ARCH** trial superior to alendronate but more serious cardiovascular events -> **avoid if MI or stroke in the past year**; follow with antiresorptive |
| **Raloxifene** | Selective oestrogen receptor modulator | Reduces **vertebral (not hip)** fractures and breast cancer; **VTE risk**, hot flushes |
| **Calcium and vitamin D** | Substrate | Adequate intake before and with all antiresorptives |

- **Sequence**: in very high-risk patients, **anabolic first, then antiresorptive** gives the greatest BMD gain; switching from denosumab to teriparatide causes bone loss (avoid).
- **Atypical femoral fracture (ASBMR task force)**: **subtrochanteric or diaphyseal**, minimal or no trauma, **transverse or short oblique** lateral-cortex fracture, non- or minimally comminuted, **medial spike** in complete fractures, **localised lateral cortical thickening ("beaking")**; often **prodromal thigh pain** and **bilateral** (image the other femur). Management: stop bisphosphonate, calcium/vitamin D, consider teriparatide; **prophylactic intramedullary nailing** for painful incomplete fractures; complete fractures treated with an IM nail (higher rates of delayed union).

### Drugs harmful to the musculoskeletal system
| Drug | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Corticosteroids** | Osteoporosis (commonest secondary cause; vertebral fractures), **osteonecrosis** (femoral head), myopathy, infection, poor wound healing |
| **Fluoroquinolones** | **Achilles tendinopathy and rupture** |
| **Heparin (long-term)** | Osteoporosis |
| **Phenytoin, carbamazepine** | Osteomalacia (vitamin D metabolism) |
| **Proton pump inhibitors** | Increased hip fracture risk |
| **Aromatase inhibitors, androgen deprivation** | Bone loss |
| **Statins** | Myopathy, rhabdomyolysis |
| **Methotrexate, vitamin A excess** | Osteopathy; impaired healing |
| **Nicotine** | Nonunion, wound infection, PJI |

## 7. Perioperative management of specific drugs
- **Antirheumatic drugs before elective THA/TKA (ACR/AAHKS 2022)**:
  - **Continue** conventional DMARDs: **methotrexate**, leflunomide, hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine (and apremilast).
  - **Withhold biologics**; schedule surgery **at the end of the dosing cycle** (e.g. adalimumab every 2 weeks -> operate in week 3).
  - **JAK inhibitors** (tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib): withhold **3 days** before surgery.
  - Restart once the **wound is healed (about 14 days)**, sutures out, and no infection.
  - **Glucocorticoids**: continue the usual daily dose; routine **supraphysiological "stress dosing" is not recommended** in patients on chronic steroids for rheumatic disease (ACR); give stress cover if hypotension or known adrenal insufficiency.
- **Warfarin**: stop **5 days** before; INR under 1.5 for surgery; bridge with LMWH only in high thrombotic risk (mechanical mitral valve, recent VTE); in hip fracture reverse with vitamin K +/- PCC to avoid delay.
- **DOACs**: stop **24-48 hours** before (longer with renal impairment and for dabigatran, and before neuraxial anaesthesia).
- **Aspirin** for secondary prevention: usually **continue**; clopidogrel stopped 5-7 days before elective surgery if safe (not in recent stents).
- **Diabetes**: omit SGLT2 inhibitors (risk of euglycaemic ketoacidosis) 2-3 days before; adjust insulin; variable-rate insulin for long fasting.
- **Sickle cell disease**: avoid hypoxia, dehydration, cold and acidosis; preoperative transfusion to Hb about 10 g/dL (TAPS trial) in HbSS; tourniquet relatively contraindicated.

## 8. Intraoperative and early postoperative emergencies
### Bone cement implantation syndrome (BCIS)
- Hypoxia, hypotension, arrhythmia or cardiac arrest around **cementation, prosthesis insertion, reduction or tourniquet release**; mechanism: **marrow and fat embolisation** (raised intramedullary pressure), plus histamine and complement release.

| Grade (Donaldson 2009) | Features |
|---|---|
| **1** | Moderate hypoxia (SpO2 under 94%) or hypotension (fall in systolic BP over 20%) |
| **2** | Severe hypoxia (SpO2 under 88%) or hypotension (systolic fall over 40%) or unexpected loss of consciousness |
| **3** | Cardiovascular collapse requiring CPR |

- Risk factors: **elderly, ASA III-IV, pulmonary hypertension, poor cardiac reserve, pathological fracture, long-stem cemented implants, osteoporosis**.
- Prevention (AAGBI/BOA/BGS 2015 guidance): identify high-risk patients, **pulsatile lavage and drying of the canal**, **retrograde cement gun insertion**, distal venting, **vigilance at cementation** (communication between surgeon and anaesthetist), adequate hydration; treat with oxygen, fluids and vasopressors.
- Cemented hemiarthroplasty remains recommended for hip fracture (NICE) despite BCIS risk.

### Fat embolism syndrome
- **24-72 hours** after long-bone (femur, tibia) or pelvic fractures; classic triad: **respiratory distress (hypoxaemia)**, **neurological changes (confusion)**, **petechial rash** (axillae, conjunctivae, oral mucosa; appears last).
- **Gurd criteria**: major - respiratory insufficiency, cerebral involvement, petechial rash; minor - tachycardia, pyrexia, retinal changes, jaundice, renal changes, anaemia, thrombocytopenia, raised ESR, fat macroglobulinaemia. **Diagnosis: at least 1 major and 4 minor**.
- Chest radiograph: bilateral fluffy infiltrates ("snowstorm"); CT brain normal; MRI brain "starfield" pattern.
- Management **supportive** (oxygen, ventilation). **Early stabilisation of long-bone fractures reduces the incidence**; prophylactic steroids are not standard (debated).

### Tourniquets
- **Pressures**: commonly **systolic + 50-75 mmHg for the upper limb** and **systolic + 100-150 mmHg for the lower limb**; or based on **limb occlusion pressure (LOP)**: **LOP + 40 mmHg (LOP under 130), + 60 (131-190), + 80 (over 190)**. **Wider cuffs need less pressure**.
- **Time**: generally **up to about 2 hours**, then deflate for a reperfusion interval if more time needed.
- **Complications**: **nerve injury** (mechanical compression **at the cuff edges**; **radial nerve** commonest in the arm), **post-tourniquet syndrome** (stiffness, pallor, weakness), skin burns from prep pooling, compartment syndrome, DVT, ischaemia-reperfusion injury.
- **On deflation**: fall in BP and central venous pressure, **rise in end-tidal CO2, potassium and lactate (metabolic acidosis)**, rise in core temperature, emboli; give prophylactic antibiotics **before** inflation.
- **Avoid exsanguination by Esmarch** in **infection and tumour** (dissemination) and suspected DVT; elevation instead.
- Relative contraindications: **sickle cell disease**, severe peripheral vascular disease, previous vascular bypass, crush injury.

### Postoperative problems
- **Delirium**: common after hip fracture (up to about one-third or more); risk factors age, dementia, polypharmacy, infection, pain, dehydration, opioids, anticholinergics, benzodiazepines. Screen (4AT, CAM); **multicomponent prevention** (orientation, hydration, mobilisation, sleep, sensory aids, analgesia, avoid catheters) and **orthogeriatric co-management**.
- **Hip fracture pathway (NICE CG124)**: surgery on the **day of or day after admission**, nerve block on arrival, cemented arthroplasty for displaced intracapsular fractures, **total hip replacement for suitable independent patients**, mobilisation the day after surgery, bone health assessment. **HIP ATTACK (Lancet 2020)**: accelerated surgery (about 6 h) vs standard (about 24 h) - no difference in mortality or major complications; observational data still link delay beyond 36-48 hours to higher mortality.
- **Enhanced recovery (ERAS)**: patient education, carbohydrate loading, short fasting (clear fluids up to 2 hours), multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia, TXA, early mobilisation (day of surgery), early removal of drains and catheters.

> Exam pearl: Cefazolin 2 g (3 g if 120 kg or more) within 60 min before incision and before the tourniquet; redose at 4 h or 1500 mL blood loss; stop within 24 h. Open fractures: antibiotics within 1 h, continue until 72 h after injury or 24 h after closure. TXA blocks lysine-binding sites on plasminogen; CRASH-2 benefit only within 3 hours.

> Exam pearl: Nitrogen bisphosphonates inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase; denosumab = anti-RANKL with rebound fractures on stopping; teriparatide is avoided in Paget disease, open physes and prior radiation; romosozumab = anti-sclerostin, avoid after recent MI/stroke. Malignant hyperthermia = RYR1, earliest sign rising end-tidal CO2, treat with dantrolene.

statistics and evidence.md:
## 1. Study designs and levels of evidence
### Observational designs
| Design | Direction | Measures | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Case report / case series** | Descriptive, no control group | Frequencies | Cheap; new conditions, rare complications | No comparison; lowest evidence (level IV) |
| **Cross-sectional** | Single point in time | **Prevalence** | Quick, cheap | Cannot establish temporal sequence (cause vs effect) |
| **Case-control** | Starts with **outcome**, looks back for exposure | **Odds ratio** | Best for **rare diseases** and long latency; quick | **Recall bias**, selection of controls; cannot give incidence |
| **Cohort (prospective)** | Starts with **exposure**, follows forward for outcome | **Incidence, relative risk** | Temporal sequence; several outcomes from one exposure | Expensive, slow, loss to follow-up; poor for rare outcomes |
| **Cohort (retrospective / historical)** | Exposure and outcome already happened; data from records | Incidence, RR | Faster, cheaper | Incomplete records, confounding |
| **Registry** | Large prospective population database (e.g. NJR, AOANJRR) | Revision rate, survivorship | Huge numbers; detects rare failures and outlier implants | Revision is a crude endpoint; limited clinical detail |

### Experimental design: the randomised controlled trial (RCT)
- **Randomisation** is the only method that balances **both known and unknown confounders**.
  - Simple, **block** (keeps group sizes equal), **stratified** (balances key prognostic factors, e.g. age, fracture type), minimisation.
- **Allocation concealment**: the person enrolling cannot know the next allocation (central computer/telephone, sequentially numbered opaque sealed envelopes). Prevents **selection bias**; distinct from blinding.
- **Blinding**: patient, surgeon, outcome assessor, analyst. In surgical trials the surgeon usually cannot be blinded; **blinded outcome assessment** is the minimum. Sham surgery trials blind the patient.
- **Intention-to-treat (ITT)**: analyse everyone in the group to which they were **randomised**, whatever treatment they received. Preserves randomisation; conservative; **the primary analysis for superiority trials**.
- **Per-protocol**: only those who completed the allocated treatment. **As-treated**: by treatment actually received. In **non-inferiority trials**, both ITT and per-protocol should show non-inferiority (ITT alone may falsely favour equivalence).
- **Superiority vs equivalence vs non-inferiority** (new treatment is not worse than standard by more than a pre-set **non-inferiority margin**; used when the new option is cheaper, safer or less invasive).
- **Explanatory** (ideal conditions, efficacy) vs **pragmatic** (real-world, effectiveness).
- **Expertise-based RCT**: patients randomised to surgeons who perform only the procedure they are expert in; removes differential expertise bias and crossovers.
- Other: **crossover** (each patient acts as own control; not suitable for surgery with permanent effect), **cluster** randomised (by hospital or surgeon), **factorial** (two interventions tested at once in a 2 x 2 design).
- Surgical RCT problems: equipoise, learning curve, blinding, standardisation of the procedure, patient preference, crossovers.
- Drug trial phases: **I** safety/dose in small numbers (often healthy volunteers); **II** efficacy and dose-finding; **III** large comparative trial before licensing; **IV** post-marketing surveillance (rare adverse effects).
- Surgical innovation: **IDEAL** framework (Idea, Development, Exploration, Assessment, Long-term study).

### Levels of evidence (JBJS, therapeutic studies)
| Level | Therapeutic studies |
|---|---|
| **I** | High-quality RCT (adequate power, follow-up at least 80%, proper randomisation) or systematic review of level I RCTs with consistent results |
| **II** | Lesser-quality RCT (e.g. under 80% follow-up, no blinding, improper randomisation), **prospective comparative (cohort) study**, systematic review of level II studies or of level I with inconsistent results |
| **III** | **Case-control study**, **retrospective comparative (cohort) study**, systematic review of level III studies |
| **IV** | **Case series** (no comparison group) |
| **V** | **Expert opinion**, mechanism-based reasoning |

- Separate hierarchies exist for **prognostic, diagnostic and economic** studies (e.g. diagnostic level I = testing previously developed criteria in consecutive patients against a universal reference standard).
- A **systematic review takes the level of the studies it includes**.

### GRADE (quality of a body of evidence)
- Four grades: **high, moderate, low, very low**.
- RCTs start **high**; observational studies start **low**.
- **Downgrade** for: risk of bias, inconsistency (heterogeneity), indirectness, imprecision (wide CI, small numbers), publication bias.
- **Upgrade** (observational) for: large effect, dose-response gradient, plausible confounding that would reduce the effect.
- AAOS guidelines grade recommendation strength as **strong, moderate, limited, consensus**.

> Exam pearl: Randomisation is the only way to control unknown confounders. Allocation concealment prevents selection bias; blinding prevents performance and detection bias. Prospective cohort = level II, retrospective cohort and case-control = level III, case series = level IV.

## 2. Bias, confounding and validity
| Bias | Meaning | Prevention |
|---|---|---|
| **Selection bias** | Groups differ systematically at baseline | Randomisation, allocation concealment, consecutive enrolment |
| **Performance bias** | Groups receive different care apart from the intervention | Blinding, standardised protocols |
| **Detection (measurement / observer) bias** | Outcome assessed differently between groups | **Blinded outcome assessor**, objective outcomes |
| **Attrition / transfer bias** | Loss to follow-up differs or is large | Follow-up at least 80% (over 20% loss threatens validity), ITT |
| **Recall bias** | Cases remember exposures better than controls (case-control) | Objective records |
| **Publication bias** | Positive studies more likely published | Trial registration, funnel plot |
| **Lead-time bias** | Earlier diagnosis seems to prolong survival (screening) | Compare from a fixed point |
| **Length-time bias** | Screening picks up slow-growing disease preferentially | RCT of screening |
| **Channelling bias** | Sicker patients steered to one treatment | Randomisation, propensity scores |
| **Hawthorne effect** | Behaviour changes because subjects know they are observed | Control group also observed |

- **Confounder**: a variable associated with both exposure and outcome, not on the causal pathway (e.g. age confounding the link between smoking and nonunion).
  - Controlled by **randomisation**, restriction, matching, stratification, **multivariable regression**, **propensity score** matching (observational studies; balances only measured confounders).
- **Effect modification (interaction)**: the effect differs across levels of a third variable (a real finding, not a bias).
- **Internal validity**: results correct for the study population. **External validity (generalisability)**: applicable to other patients.
- **Bradford Hill criteria** for causation: strength, consistency, specificity, **temporality (the only essential one)**, biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experiment, analogy.

## 3. Descriptive statistics
### Types of data
| Type | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Nominal** (categorical) | Categories without order | Sex, blood group, implant brand |
| **Ordinal** | Ordered categories, unequal intervals | Gustilo grade, Kellgren-Lawrence grade, VAS treated as ranks |
| **Interval** | Equal intervals, no true zero | Temperature in Celsius |
| **Ratio** | Equal intervals, true zero | Height, blood loss, range of motion |
| **Discrete vs continuous** | Counts vs any value | Number of revisions vs age |

### Central tendency and spread
- **Mean** (affected by outliers), **median** (middle value; for skewed or ordinal data), **mode** (commonest; nominal data).
- **Normal (Gaussian) distribution**: symmetrical, mean = median = mode.
  - **68%** within 1 SD, **95%** within **1.96 SD**, **99.7%** within 3 SD.
- **Positive (right) skew**: tail to the right, **mean > median > mode** (e.g. length of stay, hospital costs). Negative skew: mean < median < mode.
- **Standard deviation (SD)**: spread of individual values. **Variance** = SD squared.
- **Standard error of the mean (SEM) = SD / square root of n**: precision of the sample mean as an estimate of the population mean; falls as sample size rises.
- **95% confidence interval (CI)** = mean +/- 1.96 x SEM: the range that would contain the true population value in 95% of repeated samples.
- **Range and interquartile range** (25th-75th centile) for skewed data.
- Normality tested by **Shapiro-Wilk** or **Kolmogorov-Smirnov**, histograms and Q-Q plots.

## 4. Hypothesis testing
- **Null hypothesis (H0)**: no difference between groups.
- **p value**: probability of obtaining a result at least as extreme as that observed **if the null hypothesis were true**. It is **not** the probability that H0 is true and says nothing about the size or importance of the effect.
- **Significance level (alpha)** usually 0.05.

| Error | Definition | Usual value | Cause |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Type I (alpha)** | **False positive**: rejecting a true null hypothesis (finding a difference that is not there) | 0.05 | Multiple comparisons, chance |
| **Type II (beta)** | **False negative**: failing to reject a false null (missing a real difference) | 0.2 | **Small sample (underpowered)** - commonest flaw of orthopaedic studies |

- **Power = 1 - beta** (usually **80%**, sometimes 90%): the probability of detecting a real difference of a given size.
- **Sample size depends on**: alpha, power, **expected effect size** (usually the **minimal clinically important difference, MCID**), **variability (SD)** of the outcome, and expected loss to follow-up.
  - Smaller effect, larger variance, lower alpha, higher power -> **larger sample** needed.
- **Multiple comparisons** inflate type I error: **Bonferroni correction** divides alpha by the number of tests (0.05 / 5 tests = 0.01 each).
- **Confidence intervals** are more informative than p values (show magnitude and precision):
  - For a **difference** (mean difference, ARR): not significant if the CI **includes 0**.
  - For a **ratio** (RR, OR, HR): not significant if the CI **includes 1**.
- **Statistical vs clinical significance**: a tiny difference can be "significant" in a huge study; judge against the **MCID**.
- **One-tailed** tests are more powerful but only valid when a difference in one direction is impossible or irrelevant; two-tailed is standard.

## 5. Choosing the statistical test
| Data and comparison | Parametric (normal, continuous) | Non-parametric (skewed, ordinal, small n) |
|---|---|---|
| **2 independent groups** | **Unpaired (Student's) t-test** | **Mann-Whitney U** (Wilcoxon rank-sum) |
| **2 paired / related measurements** (before vs after, same patient) | **Paired t-test** | **Wilcoxon signed-rank** |
| **3 or more independent groups** | **One-way ANOVA** (then post-hoc tests) | **Kruskal-Wallis** |
| **3 or more repeated measures** | **Repeated-measures ANOVA** | **Friedman test** |
| **Association between 2 variables** | **Pearson correlation (r)** | **Spearman rank correlation (rho)** |

| Categorical outcomes | Test |
|---|---|
| **Independent groups, proportions** | **Chi-square test** |
| **Small numbers (expected count under 5 in any cell)** | **Fisher's exact test** |
| **Paired categorical data** (same patients before and after) | **McNemar test** |

### Regression and survival
- **Linear regression**: continuous outcome; **logistic regression**: binary outcome (gives **adjusted odds ratios**); multivariable models adjust for confounders.
- **Correlation coefficient (r)** -1 to +1; **r squared** = proportion of variance explained. Correlation does not prove causation.
- **Survival analysis** (time-to-event, e.g. implant revision):
  - **Kaplan-Meier** curve: survivorship with censoring (patients lost or still unrevised); steps fall at each event.
  - **Log-rank test** compares two survival curves.
  - **Cox proportional hazards regression**: adjusts for covariates; gives the **hazard ratio (HR)**.
  - **Competing risks**: in elderly patients death prevents revision; **Kaplan-Meier overestimates the cumulative revision rate**; use the **cumulative incidence function** (Fine and Gray).
  - Worst-case analysis treats lost patients as failures.
- **Benchmarks for joint replacement**: NICE (TA304, 2014) - total hip prostheses should have a revision rate (or projected rate) of **5% or less at 10 years**; **ODEP** ratings grade the strength of evidence (number of years and quality of data) that an implant meets this benchmark (e.g. 10A rating).

> Exam pearl: Paired data -> paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank; two independent groups -> unpaired t-test or Mann-Whitney U; proportions -> chi-square, or Fisher's exact when an expected cell count is under 5; implant survival -> Kaplan-Meier with log-rank, Cox for adjusted hazard ratio.

## 6. Diagnostic test statistics
### The 2 x 2 table
| | Disease present | Disease absent |
|---|---|---|
| **Test positive** | a = true positive (TP) | b = false positive (FP) |
| **Test negative** | c = false negative (FN) | d = true negative (TN) |

| Measure | Formula | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Sensitivity** | a / (a + c) | Proportion of diseased who test positive; **high sensitivity, negative result rules OUT (SnNout)** - good screening test |
| **Specificity** | d / (b + d) | Proportion of healthy who test negative; **high specificity, positive result rules IN (SpPin)** - good confirmatory test |
| **Positive predictive value (PPV)** | a / (a + b) | Probability of disease if test positive |
| **Negative predictive value (NPV)** | d / (c + d) | Probability of no disease if test negative |
| **Accuracy** | (a + d) / total | Proportion correctly classified |
| **Positive likelihood ratio (LR+)** | sensitivity / (1 - specificity) | Over 10 = strong rule-in |
| **Negative likelihood ratio (LR-)** | (1 - sensitivity) / specificity | Under 0.1 = strong rule-out |

- **Sensitivity, specificity and likelihood ratios are properties of the test** and do not change with prevalence.
- **PPV and NPV depend on prevalence**: as prevalence rises, **PPV rises and NPV falls**. A test with good specificity still has a poor PPV in a low-prevalence population.
- Likelihood ratios convert pre-test odds to post-test odds (post-test odds = pre-test odds x LR; Fagan nomogram).
- **ROC curve**: sensitivity (y-axis) against **1 - specificity** (x-axis) at different cut-offs.
  - **Area under the curve (AUC)**: 0.5 = useless (chance), 0.7-0.8 acceptable, 0.8-0.9 excellent, 1.0 perfect.
  - Optimal cut-off: point nearest the top-left corner, or maximum **Youden index (sensitivity + specificity - 1)**.
- Lowering a cut-off increases sensitivity and decreases specificity (e.g. CRP threshold for PJI).
- Using two tests **in series** (both must be positive) raises specificity; **in parallel** (either positive) raises sensitivity.

### Worked example
- 1000 patients with suspected PJI, prevalence 20% (200 infected). Test sensitivity 90%, specificity 80%.
  - TP = 180, FN = 20; TN = 640, FP = 160.
  - **PPV** = 180 / 340 = **53%**; **NPV** = 640 / 660 = **97%**.
  - LR+ = 0.9 / 0.2 = 4.5; LR- = 0.1 / 0.8 = 0.125.

## 7. Measures of association and treatment effect
- **Risk (incidence)** = events / number at risk. **Odds** = events / non-events.
- **Relative risk (RR)** = risk in exposed / risk in unexposed (cohort studies, RCTs). RR 1 = no effect.
- **Odds ratio (OR)** = ad / bc (case-control studies, logistic regression). **OR approximates RR when the outcome is rare** (under about 10%).
- **Hazard ratio (HR)**: ratio of event rates over time (survival analysis).

| Measure | Formula |
|---|---|
| **Control event rate (CER)** | events in controls / controls |
| **Experimental event rate (EER)** | events in treated / treated |
| **Absolute risk reduction (ARR)** | CER - EER |
| **Relative risk reduction (RRR)** | (CER - EER) / CER = 1 - RR |
| **Number needed to treat (NNT)** | **1 / ARR** (round up) |
| **Number needed to harm (NNH)** | 1 / absolute risk increase |

- Worked example: SSI 10% with standard care vs 5% with a new dressing: ARR = 5% (0.05), **NNT = 20**, RR = 0.5, **RRR = 50%**.
- RRR sounds impressive and stays constant; **ARR and NNT depend on baseline risk** and are clinically more meaningful.
- **Attributable risk** = incidence in exposed - incidence in unexposed.

## 8. Reliability, validity and outcome measures
### Reliability (reproducibility)
- **Intra-observer** (same observer, repeated) and **inter-observer** (different observers).
- **Cohen's kappa**: agreement between **two observers for categorical data**, corrected for chance; **weighted kappa** for ordinal data; **Fleiss kappa** for more than two observers.
- **Intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC)**: reliability of **continuous** measurements (e.g. Cobb angle).
- **Bland-Altman plot**: agreement between two measurement methods (difference plotted against mean; limits of agreement).

| Kappa (Landis and Koch) | Agreement |
|---|---|
| **Under 0** | Poor (worse than chance) |
| **0-0.20** | Slight |
| **0.21-0.40** | Fair |
| **0.41-0.60** | Moderate |
| **0.61-0.80** | Substantial |
| **0.81-1.00** | Almost perfect |

- Most fracture classifications (Neer, Garden, Gustilo, Lauge-Hansen) show only **fair to moderate** inter-observer agreement - a classic exam point.
- **Accuracy** = closeness to the true value; **precision** = reproducibility of repeated measurements.

### Validity and responsiveness of a score
- **Face, content, construct, criterion** (concurrent/predictive) validity; **responsiveness** (detects clinically important change); **floor and ceiling effects** (over 15% of patients at the lowest or highest score is a problem; e.g. ceiling effect of the Oxford knee score in high-demand patients).
- **MCID**: smallest change the patient perceives as beneficial. **PASS** (patient acceptable symptom state) and **SCB** (substantial clinical benefit) are related thresholds.

### Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs)
| Score | Type | Direction |
|---|---|---|
| **SF-36, SF-12, EQ-5D, PROMIS** | Generic health status | Higher better (EQ-5D index 1 = full health) |
| **Oxford hip / knee score** | Joint-specific, 12 items, 0-48 | **Higher better** |
| **WOMAC** | Hip and knee OA (pain, stiffness, function) | Higher worse (original scoring) |
| **KOOS, HOOS** | Knee/hip injury and OA, 0-100 | Higher better |
| **DASH, QuickDASH** | Upper limb, 0-100 | **Higher worse** (disability) |
| **Oswestry Disability Index (ODI)** | Low back, 0-100% | Higher worse |
| **Constant-Murley** | Shoulder, 100 points, includes strength (clinician measured) | Higher better |

### Health economics
- **QALY** (quality-adjusted life year) = years of life x utility (from EQ-5D).
- **Cost-utility analysis** -> **ICER** (incremental cost-effectiveness ratio) = difference in cost / difference in QALYs. NICE threshold about **20,000-30,000 pounds per QALY**.
- Cost-minimisation (equal outcomes), cost-effectiveness (natural units), cost-benefit (both in money).

## 9. Systematic reviews and meta-analysis
- **Systematic review**: explicit question (**PICO**: population, intervention, comparison, outcome), comprehensive search, predefined inclusion criteria, risk-of-bias assessment (Cochrane RoB 2 for RCTs; Newcastle-Ottawa for observational; MINORS for non-randomised surgical studies).
- **Meta-analysis**: statistical pooling of results.
- **Forest plot**: each study a **square** (point estimate; size = weight) with horizontal CI line; **diamond** = pooled estimate (width = CI); vertical **line of no effect** (1 for ratios, 0 for differences). Diamond crossing the line = not significant.
- **Heterogeneity**: **Cochran Q** and **I squared** (about 25% low, 50% moderate, 75% high).
  - **Fixed-effect** model assumes one true effect (low heterogeneity); **random-effects** model allows the true effect to vary (wider CI; used with heterogeneity).
- **Funnel plot**: effect size against precision; **asymmetry suggests publication bias** (small negative studies missing); Egger test.
- A meta-analysis of poor studies remains poor evidence ("garbage in, garbage out").

## 10. Ethics and research governance
- **Declaration of Helsinki**: ethical principles for research on humans; **informed consent**, independent ethics committee approval, protection of vulnerable groups, use of placebo only when justified.
- **Good Clinical Practice (ICH-GCP)**; in India, **ICMR National Ethical Guidelines** and prospective registration in the **Clinical Trials Registry - India (CTRI)**; ICMJE journals require **prospective registration** before enrolling the first patient.
- **Clinical equipoise**: genuine uncertainty in the expert community about which treatment is better - the ethical basis for an RCT.
- Declare **conflicts of interest**; data safety monitoring boards stop trials early for benefit, harm or futility (early stopping for benefit tends to overestimate effect).

## 11. Landmark orthopaedic RCT examples (used to test design concepts)
| Trial | Design point | Exam-relevant conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| **FAITH** (Lancet 2017) | Multicentre RCT, femoral neck fracture fixation | Sliding hip screw vs cancellous screws: no difference in reoperation overall |
| **HEALTH** (NEJM 2019) | RCT, displaced femoral neck fractures | Total hip vs hemiarthroplasty: no significant difference in secondary procedures at 2 years; slightly better function with THA |
| **ProFHER** (JAMA 2015) | Pragmatic RCT | Surgery vs sling for displaced proximal humerus fractures: no difference in Oxford shoulder score |
| **UK DRAFFT** (BMJ 2014) | Pragmatic RCT | K-wires vs volar locking plate for distal radius: no difference in PRWE at 12 months |
| **Moseley** (NEJM 2002) and **FIDELITY** (NEJM 2013) | **Sham-surgery** RCTs | Arthroscopic debridement or partial meniscectomy no better than placebo surgery for degenerative knees |
| **HIP ATTACK** (Lancet 2020) | RCT of timing | Accelerated hip fracture surgery: no reduction in mortality or major complications |

> Exam pearl: PPV and NPV change with prevalence; sensitivity, specificity and likelihood ratios do not. NNT = 1 / ARR. CI for a ratio crossing 1 or for a difference crossing 0 = not significant. Kappa for categorical agreement, ICC for continuous; Kaplan-Meier overestimates revision when death is a competing risk.
